common_name: Fredonia Grape (Early Blue Concord-Type Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Fredonia, bred at the Geneva, New York research station, ripens about two to three weeks earlier than Concord with a similar slip-skin, richly grapey flavor; best in zones 4-7 where its chill requirement is reliably met.

directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system, leaving a couple of strong canes per vine. Fredonia was bred at the Geneva, New York agricultural research station specifically to ripen earlier than Concord, giving gardeners in shorter-season climates a reliable blue slip-skin grape with the same rich, musky-sweet 'foxy' Labrusca flavor prized in grape juice and jelly. It is self-fruitful and needs no pollinator, producing large clusters of blue-black berries in late summer to early fall. Because it is a high-chill Labrusca type, it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease-tolerant muscadines or hybrid bunch grapes are more reliable choices.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties
University of Minnesota Extension — Grape Growing

common_name: Catawba Grape (Historic American Pink Wine and Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Catawba is a historic 1800s American grape with distinctive pinkish-red, musky-sweet fruit used for both fresh eating and wine; best in zones 5-8 where its chill requirement is reliably met.

directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Catawba is one of the oldest named American grape varieties, discovered in North Carolina in the early 1800s and once the most widely planted wine grape in the country, producing distinctive coppery-pink to reddish-purple berries with the characteristic musky, richly sweet Labrusca 'foxy' flavor, used historically for sparkling and still wine as well as fresh eating and juice. It is self-fruitful and ripens in mid to late season. As a high-chill Labrusca type it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease pressure and insufficient winter chill limit its success; Gulf South growers do better with muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties
University of Minnesota Extension — Grape Growing

common_name: Delaware Grape (Historic Small-Berried American Pink Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Delaware, a historic mid-1800s American grape, bears small, sweet, pink-red berries long valued for high-quality wine as well as fresh eating; best in zones 5-8 where its chill requirement is reliably met.

directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Delaware is a historic American grape dating to the mid-1800s, producing small, tightly clustered, pink-red berries with notably high sugar content and a delicate, sweet, wine-quality flavor considered superior to many other Labrusca-type grapes of its era, and it remains valued today for both fresh eating and wine and juice production. It is self-fruitful and matures in midseason. As a high-chill Labrusca type it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties
University of Minnesota Extension — Grape Growing

common_name: Diamond Grape (Moore's Diamond, Historic White American Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Diamond, also called Moore's Diamond, is an 1880s American white grape valued for its mild, sweet flavor and good disease resistance for a Labrusca-type grape; best in zones 5-8 where its chill requirement is reliably met.

directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Diamond, also known as Moore's Diamond, is a white American grape introduced in the 1880s, producing greenish-yellow berries in compact clusters with a mild, sweet flavor much less pronounced in the musky 'foxy' Labrusca character than many other American grapes, making it a pleasant fresh-eating and juice grape as well as a wine grape valued for delicate white wines. It is self-fruitful and ripens in early to midseason with good vigor and disease resistance for its type. As a high-chill Labrusca-derived grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties
University of Minnesota Extension — Grape Growing
